title: The Kazi Schooled By His Wife

keywords: the kazi schooled by his wife
full_text:
In Cairo presided a venerable Kazi named Abu Tahir, who was an absolute master of legal texts, statutes, and ancient commentaries. Yet in his judgments, he was excessively rigid, ignoring human circumstances and imposing mechanical fines on the poorest litigants.

His wife, Lady Sitt al-Qudat, was a woman of extraordinary intelligence and practical insight.
One evening at dinner, Abu Tahir boasted:
'No jurist in Egypt understands the science of law better than I. My verdicts are infallible!'

Lady Sitt al-Qudat smiled quietly. The next morning, she disguised herself in the heavy veil of a poor widow, went to her husband's public court, and presented a complaint:
'O Chief Kazi! I have a neighbor who owns a magnificent, fertile grapevine. The vines have grown over the wall into my modest courtyard. Every autumn, ripe clusters fall upon my paving stones. My neighbor claims that because the roots are in his soil, the fallen fruit belongs to him, and demands I pay him twenty silver dirhams for the grapes my hungry children ate. What is your judgment?'

Abu Tahir stroked his beard, opened his heavy law books, and pronounced sternly:
'The law is clear! The tree follows the root! The fallen fruit belongs to the owner of the trunk. Thou must pay twenty dirhams or go to debtors' prison!'

The veiled woman bowed, walked out, and returned home.
That evening, when Abu Tahir sat down to his lavish dinner, he found his plate containing only dry bread crusts and a cup of cold water.
He frowned: 'Where is the roasted chicken? Where is the saffron rice with pine nuts?'

Sitt al-Qudat sat opposite him, smiling calmly:
'Husband, the money I had for the market was paid to the neighbor whose grape cluster fell into our courtyard! For according to the Chief Kazi's brilliant verdict this morning, we owe him twenty dirhams!'

Abu Tahir stared at his wife, recognizing her voice and her eyes beneath the veil.
She looked at him with profound gentleness:
'Abu Tahir, thou art wise in books, but blind in life. When a tree overhangs another's wall, its shade and fruit are heaven's gift of neighborly love, not a cause for prison. If law does not serve mercy and common sense, it is only a blunt instrument that starves the innocent.'

Abu Tahir blushed, dropped his head in profound humility, and embraced his wife.
From that day forward, the Kazi never issued a verdict without considering human compassion, becoming celebrated throughout Egypt as the most humane and beloved judge of his generation.
moral: Theoretical knowledge of law is useless without practical justice and empathy for the human heart.
